name: Don't shave: hair-growth encouragement for body

lead: In chest-hair-maxxing communities, not shaving means leaving chest, torso and limb hair to reach its natural length so its full density shows, as part of looking more masculine. Some practitioners also say shaving makes hair come back coarser or patchier and that stopping lets the true pattern show.

Reference sources report that shaving does not change the thickness, colour or rate of regrowth of terminal hair; the blunt cut end and lack of sun-lightening can make regrowth look different. Body hair is described in the endocrine literature as dependent on androgens and on how sensitive follicles are to them, so density is set mainly by hormones, genetics and age.

paras: People stop shaving, waxing or trimming the area and let hair grow for months, sometimes alongside other efforts to look more masculine. Hair reaches its natural length and shows what is there.

Not shaving carries no medical risk in itself. Hair that is thin or patchy may stay so, and the topic overlaps with discussion of minoxidil, hormones and transplants for body hair, which carry their own risks.

angle.text: Chest-hair-maxxing communities leave body hair untrimmed so it reaches its natural length and shows its full density, a more masculine look. Some also believe shaving thickens regrowth; sources that address this report it does not, and density is mostly androgens and genetics.

lead: 'Don't shave' is a practice in the chest-hair-maxxing corner of looksmaxxing culture: leaving chest, torso and limb hair untrimmed so it reaches its natural length and density. Proponents treat body hair as a secondary sexual characteristic and want it as visible as possible, so abstaining from razors, trimmers and wax is usually the first and free step before anything else is tried.

Medical literature describes body hair as androgen-dependent: scalp hair grows without androgens, whereas body hair requires them [1]. How much body hair a person has is shaped by androgen levels, by how sensitive follicles are to androgens, by age and by population background [1][2]. Shaving is not described in these sources as altering that capacity.

General reference sources report that shaving does not make terminal hair grow back thicker, coarser or darker, and attribute the impression to the blunt cut tip, to shorter hairs being stiffer, and to the lack of sun-lightening on freshly grown hair [3]. For people who have shaved for years, growing hair out also removes the shaving-related skin irritation described below. No controlled study has examined 'not shaving' as an appearance strategy.

paras: The practice consists of not shaving, trimming or waxing the chest, abdomen and limbs, and letting hair grow for a period, often several months, before judging the result. Participants in chest-hair threads typically describe it as a first step before trying topical, hormonal or surgical options, and as a way of finding out the baseline pattern: where the hair is dense, where it is patchy and how it grows in direction and length.

Related choices that people discuss alongside it include tidying only the neckline, trimming to a uniform length rather than removing hair, and treating the chest as part of overall physique presentation together with training and body fat.

Before puberty most body hair is fine, pale vellus hair. Rising androgens, mainly testosterone and its derivative dihydrotestosterone, convert follicles in many regions into producing darker, thicker terminal hair, with chest and abdominal hair increasing in men from late puberty into adulthood [2]. Body hair also has a shorter growth phase than scalp hair, which is one reason it stops at a finite length [2]. Review literature states that body hair growth depends on androgens, in contrast to scalp hair [1].

Hair patterns vary between individuals and populations. Studies of hirsutism in women show that the amount of terminal body hair in the general population varies with ethnicity [4][5], and a classic clinical scoring method grades hair growth by body region [6]. Comparative work summarised in encyclopedic sources reports that differences in follicle sensitivity, including to the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase, probably explain part of the variation, and that hairiness differs between populations even at similar androgen levels [2]. 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone and is described as one contributor to androgen action in hair follicles [7][8]. Research on testosterone treatment in trans men documents increased body and facial hair as an effect of androgen exposure [9].

The idea that shaving thickens regrowth is widely repeated. Reference sources explain why it feels true: an uncut hair has a tapered tip while a cut one ends bluntly and can feel coarser, shorter hairs are stiffer than longer ones, and hair that has not yet been bleached by sun can look darker [3]. Hair also tends to become coarser and spread to more areas with age, so adolescents who begin shaving at around the same time as puberty changes may attribute the changes to the razor [3].

Proponents of not shaving often describe their experience in these terms: after stopping, the hair looks softer at the tip and more even, and the pattern that was hidden by stubble becomes clear. Whether this reflects anything beyond the cut-tip effect has not been tested.

Shaving is associated with razor burn, an irritation linked with dry shaving, pressing hard or using a dull blade, and with ingrown hairs and razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae), a persistent inflammation caused by shaving [3]. Guidance summarised there lists shaving with the grain, lubrication and fresh blades, and notes that multi-blade razors can irritate by cutting very close [3]. Not shaving avoids these effects on the chest and torso.

Chest hair is discussed in appearance forums as part of masculine frame, and not shaving is commonly listed as the free first step in chest-hair guides. Community members who report poor density usually move on to discussion of hormones, minoxidil applied to the chest, or body hair transplants, which are separate topics with their own risks. Wikipedia notes that athletes such as swimmers, cyclists and bodybuilders may shave body hair for friction or to show muscle definition [2], and bodybuilding-influenced communities sometimes discuss the opposite preference for a natural look.

No studies found on abstaining from shaving as a way to increase body hair. The related endocrine research above concerns androgen action and hirsutism scoring rather than grooming behaviour [6][1][4][9].

lore.intro: Chest hair is discussed in appearance forums as part of masculine frame, and not shaving is often listed as the free first step in 'chest hair maxxing' guides. Community accounts are anecdotal.
